facts.fact: Iranian MRI study (midline, Iranian sample): mid-philtrum soft tissue thickness averaged 16.41 mm in males vs 13.95 mm in females; males had thicker tissue at most midline landmarks.
Iranian MRI midline study: nasion thickness rose with BMI from 5.57 mm in the lowest BMI group to 8.25 mm in the highest BMI group; thickness increased with BMI at several landmarks.
Nigerian adult female community study (CT-based midline): mean midphiltrum 10.80 mm and labiomental 11.79 mm.
Greek adult population CT study (22 landmarks: 5 midsagittal, 17 bilateral): age and sex had a limited effect on soft tissue depth at these landmarks.

Greek CT study inter-observer TEM values ranged 0.19 to 1.45 mm; the authors judged repeated measurements at 22 landmarks unreliable for inter-observer error (attribution to this paper inferred from search snippet).
Thai ultrasound study (above middle age, ultrasonographic imaging): significant FSTT differences across all landmarks between underweight and normal BMI groups; BMI had a notable effect.

Thai ultrasound study: females were thicker at several sites while males were thicker in nasal and perioral regions (sex effect is site-dependent); aging had minimal impact on FSTT in individuals over 50.

Ultrasound facial skin (dermal) thickness study: at the mid-cheek, dermal thickness was 1.877 mm in males and 1.580 mm in females; epidermal thickness did not differ significantly by sex and skin thickness did not correlate significantly with BMI. This measures skin layer only, not total soft tissue depth.
Forensic systematic review (2023) screened 84 articles; 30 presented databases on sex, age and ethnicity-dependent soft tissue thickness variation.

Pooled review of FSTT literature: 139 studies published since 1883, over 220,000 measurements from more than 19,500 adults; the pooled T-Tables were first calculated in 2008 and are still used as means for superimposition and approximation.
NCJRS abstract: a pooled soft-tissue-depth table built from 66 studies, analysed by year, measurement method, race and sex; reports wide variation between measurement techniques.
Korean CBCT database: 100 adults (50 men, 50 women) measured at 31 landmarks; most landmarks thicker in men.

Chinese layer-specific CT study: 1174 adults aged 18-90 measured at 33 landmarks, with skin, fat and muscle layers separated; sex and age significantly affected total thickness and fat and muscle layers.
Yangtze River delta Han CBCT study: 424 adults, 60 landmarks from 3D models; examined sex, age, BMI and malocclusion effects.
Central Chinese CT study: 280 individuals, 41 landmarks, total soft tissue and fat thickness recorded.

Brazilian CBCT study (100 scans, 32 landmarks): 'perpendicular to bone' measurement method gave high inter- and intra-observer reproducibility at all 32 landmarks, while 'perpendicular to skin' and 'direct' methods had low reproducibility; authors suggest identifying landmarks on hard-tissue images.
CBCT reliability study used 11 landmarks marked with dermal punch holes; CBCT of the face was judged reliable for soft tissue thickness (ICC and absolute error used).
Linear scleroderma CBCT study: mean ICC for soft tissue thickness was 0.49 in patients vs 0.66 in controls.
A CBCT review recommended a 0.3 mm voxel size for accurate facial soft tissue measurement and noted CBCT has weaker soft-tissue differentiation than CT and MRI.

De Greef et al. (2006) in vivo facial soft tissue depth measurements on 967 adult Caucasoids; CT-derived values from total head CT scans of twelve patients (attribution inferred from a Leuven abstract snippet; original paper not retrieved).
Average soft tissue thickness values are typically measured at a sparse set of fewer than 53 landmarks, which motivates denser approaches.

Gietzen et al. (PLOS ONE 2019, cited via arXiv 1808.07334) build a dense FSTT statistic by registering a skull model to each CT-extracted skull and computing thickness per vertex toward the extracted skin surface.

Skull-to-Face (2024) learns the joint distribution of tissue thickness at skull landmarks from scanned skull-face pairs; model complexity is limited by the small paired dataset; CT scans at 0.25 mm/pixel.
Orthodontic-profile paper (PMC12532767) notes BMI is the variable most strongly associated with FSTT among age, sex and BMI, and FSTT tends to decrease over time with reduced muscle tone.
Pediatric systematic review (PRISMA) concludes soft tissue thickness is significantly greater in obese individuals (ages 6-18).
Scoping review of Brazilian facial approximation methods flags standardization of landmarks and validation of FSTT tables as open challenges.

Critique: mean-depth tables are weakest at nose, mouth and ears, which have little direct skeletal support; a computerized approach found weaker correlations and greater errors for nose and mouth shapes.
Critique of needle-probe method: needle pressure distorts soft-tissue depth; supine CT/MRI positioning may introduce error.

Stephan (2007 AAFS abstract) argues traditional ancestry/classification of soft tissue depth data has little empirical statistical justification; pooled tables do not separately retain sex, ancestry, body position or measurement method.
Rhine and Moore (1984) published tissue thickness tables for American Caucasoids (Maxwell Museum Technical Series 1); no independent validation against modern samples was found.
Flynn (1989) cephalometric study reports soft tissue norms for black vs white American adults, with greater soft-tissue chin thickness in the black sample (secondary Scribd copy only).
Mastoid CT study: male sex associated with thicker tissue, adjusted difference 1.37 mm; age not independently associated (source URL not confirmed in results).

contradictions: Sex effect is not uniform: Iranian MRI and Korean CBCT report males thicker at most landmarks, while the Thai ultrasound study reports females thicker at several sites and males only in nasal and perioral regions.
Age effect: Greek CT reports limited age and sex effects, while the Chinese 1174-adult CT study reports significant sex and age effects on total thickness.
Cadaver vs living: a 50-cadaver Japanese MDCT study found earlier cadaveric data thinner at nearly all sites than earlier living Japanese data (secondary report; source not confirmed).
Race/ancestry: Stephan argues ancestry categories lack statistical justification, while the Rhine and Moore tables and Flynn (1989) use ancestry-specific values; no direct test found.
Interobserver: Greek CT study judged its inter-observer error unreliable, while a 2D vs 3D comparison found inter- and intra-observer error not significantly different.
openQuestions: Stephan 2009 T-table mm values were not retrieved; the T-table numbers must be fetched from the original paper or the 2023 IJLM review.
De Greef 2006 per-landmark mean values were not retrieved; only sample size (967 in vivo, 12 CT) confirmed by a snippet.
No ultrasound study of total facial soft tissue depth was found; only skin-layer ultrasound data.
Japanese postmortem CT (103 cadavers, ages 18-86) and Greek 100-scan CT (50M/50F, ages 18-99) are referenced but their primary URLs were not confirmed in results.
Measurement-method effects (supine CT vs upright, needle probe vs imaging) lack quantitative sources in this pass.
No direct MRI vs CBCT vs CT agreement study was found.
Fetching was not attempted (sandbox limit), so all figures rely on search snippets and should be verified against full text.
